**Components fixed by the examples**

- **X4 = both are 1, Y1 = bit 1, Z3: true → green, false → blue.** In X4-Y1-Z3, every green input has bit 1 equal to 1 in both stimuli, and no blue input does. No other bit and rule fits.
- **Y3 = bit 2, Z1: true → yellow, false → green.** In X4-Y3-Z1, every yellow input has bit 2 equal to 1 in both stimuli, and no green input does.
- **X5 = not both are 1, Y4 = bit 3.** In X5-Y4-Z3, every blue (false) input has bit 3 equal to 1 in both stimuli. Bit 4 does not fit.
- **Y2 = bit 4.** In X3-Y2-Z4, yellow appears exactly when bit 4 is the same in both stimuli. So X3 is either "same" (yellow when true) or "exactly one" (blue when true).
- **X2 and X6 share Z2.** In X2-Y3-Z2, yellow appears exactly when bit 2 is 0 in both stimuli. In X6-Y3-Z2, yellow appears exactly when bit 2 is the same in both stimuli.

**The two assignments that fit**

Different versions must have different meanings, so only two complete assignments work:

| | X2 | X6 | X3 | Z2 true | Z4 true | Z4 false |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | neither is 1 | same | exactly one | yellow | blue | yellow |
| B | at least one | exactly one | same | blue | yellow | blue |

Nothing in the examples separates A from B.

**The new task X4-Y4-Z4**

The rule is "bit 3 is 1 in both stimuli." Under B it gives yellow when true and blue when false. Under A every answer is flipped. Inputs 3, 4, 11 and 15 have bit 3 equal to 1 in both stimuli. I arbitrarily chose B, so those four are yellow and the rest are blue.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: red, green, blue, or yellow. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> blue` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is blue.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
